claim: Spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a physiologically relevant form of Hebbian learning.
source: Spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a physiologically relevant form of Hebbian learning (Caporale and Dan, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caporale and Dan, 2008

claim: In classic STDP, pre-before-post spike pairings induce timing-dependent long-term potentiation (t-LTP).
source: In its classic form, STDP depends on the order and precise timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes: pre-before-post spike pairings induce timing-dependent long-term potentiation (t-LTP), whereas post-before-pre pairings induce timing-dependent long-term depression (t-LTD) (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Markram et al., 1997 and Bi and Poo, 1998

claim: In classic STDP, post-before-pre spike pairings induce timing-dependent long-term depression (t-LTD).
source: In its classic form, STDP depends on the order and precise timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes: pre-before-post spike pairings induce timing-dependent long-term potentiation (t-LTP), whereas post-before-pre pairings induce timing-dependent long-term depression (t-LTD) (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Markram et al., 1997 and Bi and Poo, 1998

claim: The quantitative rules of STDP are profoundly influenced by neuromodulators.
source: However, the quantitative rules of STDP are profoundly influenced by neuromodulators (Seol et al., 2007; Pawlak et al., 2010), including dopamine (DA) (Zhang et al., 2009; Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Yang and Dani, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seol et al., 2007 and Pawlak et al., 2010

claim: Dopamine influences the quantitative rules of STDP.
source: However, the quantitative rules of STDP are profoundly influenced by neuromodulators (Seol et al., 2007; Pawlak et al., 2010), including dopamine (DA) (Zhang et al., 2009; Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Yang and Dani, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2009; Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Yang and Dani, 2014

claim: Reward-motivated behavior depends on the activity of dopamine neurons.
source: Although it is well established that reward-motivated behavior depends on the activity of DA neurons (Schultz et al., 1997; Suri and Schultz, 1999; Pan et al., 2005), the mechanisms that associate specific experiences with rewarding outcomes, which typically occur after a delay, are not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schultz et al., 1997; Suri and Schultz, 1999; Pan et al., 2005

claim: The mechanisms that associate specific experiences with rewarding outcomes that occur after a delay are not well understood.
source: Although it is well established that reward-motivated behavior depends on the activity of DA neurons (Schultz et al., 1997; Suri and Schultz, 1999; Pan et al., 2005), the mechanisms that associate specific experiences with rewarding outcomes, which typically occur after a delay, are not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge

claim: The problem of associating experiences with delayed rewards is referred to as the distal reward problem.
source: This is referred to as the distal reward problem (Hull, 1943).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hull, 1943

claim: Pre-before-post pairing protocol with Δt = +10 ms induced t-LTP (182 ± 14%).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Bi and Poo, 1998; Zhang et al., 2009; Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011), the pre-before-post pairing protocol with Δt = +10 ms induced t-LTP (182 ± 14%; t(4) = 5.6, p = 0.0049 vs 100%, n = 5; Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figure 1A

claim: Post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms induced t-LTD (61 ± 9%).
source: the post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms induced t-LTD (61 ± 9%; t(4) = 4.4, p = 0.0121 vs 100%, n = 5; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figure 1B

claim: Post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −10 ms elicited robust t-LTP (202 ± 21%).
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that the post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −10 ms instead of inducing t-LTD, elicited robust t-LTP (202 ± 21%; t(6) = 5.0, p = 0.0025 vs 100%, n = 7; Figure 1C,D,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 1C, D, G

claim: The finding that post-before-pre pairing with Δt = −10 ms induces t-LTP conflicts with previous reports from hippocampal cultures and acute slices.
source: This conflicts with previous reports from hippocampal cultures (Bi and Poo, 1998; Zhang et al., 2009) and acute slices (Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Yang and Dani, 2014), where post-before-pre pairing protocols never elicited synaptic potentiation in baseline conditions.
evidence: Comparison with cited literature

claim: Dopamine has been found to widen the time window for the induction of t-LTP.
source: Given that DA has been found to widen the time window for the induction of t-LTP (Zhang et al., 2009; Yang and Dani, 2014), we wanted to assess whether endogenous DA could be responsible for the potentiation observed with the post-before-pre pairing under our experimental conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2009 and Yang and Dani, 2014

claim: Combined application of D1/D5 receptor antagonist SCH23390 (10 μM) and D2-like receptor antagonist sulpiride (50 μM) prevented t-LTP and enabled t-LTD instead (72 ± 8%) at Δt = −10 ms.
source: Indeed, combined application of the D1/D5 receptor antagonist SCH23390 (10 μM) and D2-like receptor antagonist sulpiride (50 μM) from the start of the recordings prevented t-LTP and enabled t-LTD instead (72 ± 8%; t(5) = 3.6, p = 0.0160 vs 100%, n = 6; Figure 1C,D,G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 1C, D, G

claim: Endogenous dopamine, presumably released during the pairing protocol, results in changed polarity of plasticity at narrow negative spike-timing intervals.
source: These results suggest a modulatory action of endogenous DA, presumably released during the pairing protocol (Frey et al., 1990; Yang and Dani, 2014), which resulted in the changed polarity of plasticity at narrow negative spike-timing intervals.
evidence: Inference from experimental results with supporting citations

claim: Post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms elicited robust t-LTD (74 ± 9%) in control condition.
source: Indeed, the post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms, which elicited robust t-LTD in control condition (74 ± 9%, t(8) = 3.0, p = 0.0165 vs 100%, n = 9; Figure 1E–G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 1E-G

claim: Exogenous dopamine (20 μM) applied during post-before-pre pairings with Δt = −20 ms induced significant t-LTP (144 ± 12%).
source: induced significant t-LTP when exogenous DA (20 μM) was bath-applied for 10–12 min from 2 min before and during the post-before-pre pairings in interleaved experiments (144 ± 12%; t(5) = 3.7, p = 0.0148 vs 100%, n = 6; Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 1E-G

claim: The presence of dopamine during coordinated spiking activity widens the spike time interval for induction of t-LTP.
source: Therefore, in accordance with previous findings (Zhang et al., 2009; Yang and Dani, 2014), the presence of DA during the coordinated spiking activity widens the spike time interval for induction of t-LTP.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental data with supporting citations

claim: Exogenous dopamine (100 μM) applied within 1 min after post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms converted t-LTD into t-LTP (169 ± 16%).
source: Exogenous DA (100 μM) added to the perfusion system for 10–12 min starting within 1 min after the post-before-pre pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms converted t-LTD into t-LTP (169 ± 16%, t(5) = 4.3, p = 0.0078 vs 100%, n = 6; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 2A, B

claim: Dopamine can have a retroactive effect allowing negative spike pairings to induce t-LTP.
source: This implies that DA can have a retroactive effect allowing negative spike pairings to induce t-LTP.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

claim: The conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP is due to specific dopamine receptor activation.
source: Thus, the conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP was due to specific DAR activation.
evidence: Inference from antagonist experiments

claim: When the test pathway was not stimulated following the pairing protocol until after dopamine washout, robust t-LTD was induced (61 ± 5%).
source: Importantly, when the test pathway was not stimulated following the pairing protocol until after DA washout (stimulation resumed 15 min after pairing), robust t-LTD was induced (61 ± 5%, t(5) = 8.1, p = 0.0005 vs 100%, n = 6; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 2A, B

claim: The effect of dopamine is activity dependent.
source: The effect of DA was, therefore, activity dependent, demonstrating that the reinforcing signal is capable of acting specifically on the active inputs.
evidence: Inference from experimental results showing requirement for stimulation

claim: Dopamine had no significant effect on basal Schaffer-collateral transmission (110 ± 7%) without pairing with postsynaptic action potentials.
source: Consistent with earlier reports (Otmakhova and Lisman, 1999), DA had no significant effect on the basal Schaffer-collateral transmission (110 ± 7%, t(7) = 1.4, p = 0.2169 vs 100%, n = 8; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis, citation, and Figures 2A, B

claim: Application of dopamine 10 min after post-before-pre pairing caused a reversal of t-LTD back to baseline (94 ± 9%).
source: Application of DA 10 min after the post-before-pre pairing caused a reversal of t-LTD back to baseline (94 ± 9%, t(11) = 0.7, p = 0.5230 vs 100%, n = 12; Figure 3B,D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 3B, D

claim: Application of dopamine 30 min after post-before-pre pairing failed to influence t-LTD (59 ± 12%).
source: whereas application of DA 30 min after the post-before-pre pairing failed to influence t-LTD altogether (59 ± 12%, t(5) = 3.4, p = 0.0200 vs 100%, n = 6; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 3C, D

claim: Dopamine applied after the induction of low frequency stimulation-induced LTD can reduce the magnitude of synaptic depression.
source: Whilst it has previously been reported that DA applied after the induction of low frequency stimulation-induced LTD can reduce the magnitude of synaptic depression (Mockett et al., 2007), our data demonstrate, for the first time to our knowledge, that DA can change the polarity of STDP when acting within a short time window following the induction protocol.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mockett et al., 2007

claim: Dopamine can change the polarity of STDP when acting within a short time window following the induction protocol.
source: Whilst it has previously been reported that DA applied after the induction of low frequency stimulation-induced LTD can reduce the magnitude of synaptic depression (Mockett et al., 2007), our data demonstrate, for the first time to our knowledge, that DA can change the polarity of STDP when acting within a short time window following the induction protocol.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study

claim: Both hippocampal t-LTP and t-LTD require functional NMDA receptors.
source: Both hippocampal t-LTP and t-LTD (Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Yang and Dani, 2014), as well as the modulation of STDP by DA (Zhang et al., 2009), require functional NMDA receptors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011 and Yang and Dani, 2014

claim: The modulation of STDP by dopamine requires functional NMDA receptors.
source: Both hippocampal t-LTP and t-LTD (Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Yang and Dani, 2014), as well as the modulation of STDP by DA (Zhang et al., 2009), require functional NMDA receptors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009

claim: Application of d-AP5 (50 μM) after post-before-pre pairing protocol did not affect the development of t-LTD (57 ± 12%).
source: Application of the NMDA receptor antagonist d-2-amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (d-AP5, 50 μM) after the post-before-pre pairing protocol did not by itself affect the development of t-LTD (57 ± 12%, t(5) = 3.6, p = 0.0156 vs 100%, n = 6, Δt = −20 ms; Figure 4A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 4A, D

claim: Dopamine in the presence of d-AP5 reversed t-LTD back to baseline but failed to convert t-LTD into t-LTP (105 ± 12%).
source: Nevertheless, DA in the presence of d-AP5 reversed t-LTD back to baseline albeit failing to convert t-LTD into t-LTP (105 ± 12%, t(5) = 0.4, p = 0.6898 vs 100%, n = 6, Δt = −20 ms; Figure 4A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 4A, D

claim: There is a dissociation between two mechanisms involved in DA-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP: reversal of synaptic depression (de-depression) and synaptic potentiation, one of which is NMDA receptor dependent.
source: This suggests an important dissociation between two mechanisms involved in the DA-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTD, namely a reversal of synaptic depression (de-depression) and synaptic potentiation, one of which is NMDA receptor dependent.
evidence: Inference from d-AP5 experiments showing partial blockade

claim: Forskolin (50 μM) applied immediately after pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms resulted in robust conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP (167 ± 17%).
source: We found that the general AC activator, forskolin (50 μM), applied for 10–12 min immediately after the pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms resulted in robust conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP (167 ± 17%, t(6) = 3.9, p = 0.0078 vs 100%, n = 7; Figure 4B,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 4B, D

claim: Forskolin (50 μM) applied in the absence of pairing protocol had no significant effect on baseline EPSPs (83 ± 12%).
source: Notably, forskolin (50 μM) applied in the absence of the pairing protocol had no significant effect on baseline EPSPs (83 ± 12%, t(6) = 1.4, p = 0.2046 vs 100%, n = 7; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Bath application of d-AP5 (50 μM) before forskolin treatment prevented synaptic potentiation from developing, although synaptic depression was reversed (102 ± 11%).
source: The forskolin-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP was also NMDA receptor dependent since bath application of d-AP5 (50 μM) 1 min before forskolin treatment prevented synaptic potentiation from developing, although synaptic depression was reversed (102 ± 11%, t(5) = 0.2, p = 0.8616 vs 100%, n = 6; Figure 4B,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 4B, D

claim: The cAMP cascade works either upstream of or in parallel to NMDA receptor activation for the development of potentiation.
source: This result suggests that the cAMP cascade works either upstream of or in parallel to NMDA receptor activation for the development of potentiation to occur.
evidence: Inference from forskolin and d-AP5 experiments

claim: The PKA inhibitor H-89 (20 µM) blocked the DA-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP, resulting in significant t-LTD (76 ± 5%).
source: Downstream of cAMP, PKA is involved because the PKA inhibitor, H-89 (20 µM), blocked the DA-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP, revealing significant t-LTD (76 ± 5%, t(6) = 5.0, p = 0.0025 vs 100%, n = 7; Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and Figures 4C, D

claim: The DA-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP involves activation of the cAMP/PKA signaling cascade.
source: Taken together, these results imply that the DA-induced conversion of t-LTD into t-LTP involves activation of the cAMP/PKA signaling cascade, which closely mimics the effects of DA (Figure 4A vs Figure 4B).
evidence: Inference from forskolin and H-89 experiments

claim: D2-like receptor stimulation can potentiate adenylyl cyclase activity.
source: Although, D2-like receptors are typically associated with the inhibition of AC (Neve et al., 2004), interestingly, there is also evidence that D2-like receptor stimulation can potentiate AC activity (Glass and Felder, 1997; Watts and Neve, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glass and Felder, 1997 and Watts and Neve, 1997

claim: D2-like receptors are typically associated with the inhibition of adenylyl cyclase.
